title: America 250 and the Imperial Nation
author: Daniel Falcone
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/the-new-york-
public-library-uLrU12CekPY-unsplash-680x487.jpg)

Image by New York Public Library.

The renowned political theorist [Danielle
Allen](https://danielleallen.scholars.harvard.edu/) once
[wrote](https://wwnorton.com/books/Our-Declaration/), “The Declaration of
Independence matters because it helps us to see that we cannot have freedom
_without_ equality.” As the United States commemorates the 250th anniversary
of its independence on July 4, 2026, the [Declaration of
Independence](https://www.archives.gov/founding-docs/declaration-transcript)
(1776), the [U.S. Constitution](https://www.archives.gov/founding-
docs/constitution-transcript) (1787) and [Northwest
Ordinance](https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/northwest-ordinance)
(1787) link early concepts of imperial power, sovereignty, legitimacy, and
interdependence. Combining these three documents is a departure from the
historiography that sometimes places American imperialism starting in the
nineteenth century and in the context of Westward expansion or U.S. pursuit of
places like Alaska (1867) and Hawaii (1898); the latter two in accordance with
the “[blue water thesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_water_thesis)” of
imperialism.[[1]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-1) I
argue that the founding principles of the country were rooted in colonization
and imperialism more so than freedom and liberation. In other words, the
process of colonization started much earlier than the 1800s.

The U.S. started out as both a republic and an empire in the 1700s. As scholar
Greg Grandin recently pointed out, “[American freedom was built on endless
conquest](https://jacobin.com/2026/06/libertys-brutal-conquest).” This was
evident in its territorial expansion and indigenous dispossession that were
built into its early stages. “We have it in our power to begin the world over
again,” wrote [Thomas
Paine](https://www.nytimes.com/2005/07/31/books/review/thomas-paine-and-the-
promise-of-america-founding-father-of-the.html) in 1776. Paine was a rarity,
as the lone progressive Founding Father in that he envisioned domestic liberty
and not an empire. His contemporaries, at best, however, saw native people as
obstacles and children to be disciplined when they were not steered for
diplomatic purposes. At worst, they were to be removed or slaughtered
outright. In 1776, the [_First Report on
Canada_](https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Papers_of_Thomas_Jefferson_Volume_1/ZRCnDwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=First+Report+on+the+Committee+to+Digest+the+Resolutions+Respecting+Canada+and+Indian+Allies+1776&pg=PA389&printsec=frontcover)
stated its purpose as a territorial
strategy.[[2]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-2) Even
with the [Articles of Confederation](https://www.archives.gov/milestone-
documents/articles-of-confederation) (1777) there was acknowledgement of
indigenous sovereignty, but at the same time, speculation over the future of
“Indian
affairs.”[[3]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-3)

Historians such as [Fr. Francis Paul
Prucha](https://www.historians.org/perspectives-article/father-francis-paul-
prucha-sj-1921-2015-december-2015/), [Colin G.
Calloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_G._Calloway), and [Robert J.
Williams, Jr.](https://www.elmhurst.edu/news/robert-williams-jr-discusses-
native-american-law/), documented the shift in the colonial perspective from
strategic ally and brothers in liberty, to children and domestically dependent
nations. Native Americans went from equals to those in need of
guardianship.[[4]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-4)
The [Treaty of Paris](https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/treaty-of-
paris) (1783) further undermined Indian sovereignty and legitimacy and allowed
indigenous ancestral lands to be transferred without native peoples’ consent.
Recent scholarship pays more attention to the [Northwest
Ordinance](https://academic.oup.com/jah/article-
abstract/111/1/15/7695600?redirectedFrom=fulltext), drafted mainly by
[Manasseh Cutler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manasseh_Cutler), [Rufus
King](https://www.senate.gov/senators/FeaturedBios/Featured_Bio_KingRufus.htm)
and [Nathan Dane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Dane), over the
Constitution, and points to the direct expansionist policies it structured
culturally through America’s founding documents and
strategies.[[5]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-5)

The U.S. was also _intended_ to be both a republic and an empire. The
Ordinance was used to organize and pacify white settlers and protect their
interests from the big planter class. Further, since [James
Madison](https://history.state.gov/departmenthistory/people/madison-james)
favored orderly expansion and feared direct democracy he “used [the Ordinance]
as a tool of settler colonial expropriation and violence against indigenous
peoples and their homelands. That it served the ends of white supremacy,
however, can obscure the fact that much of its essential work was directed at,
not on behalf of, white men, specifically to harness and direct the polities
they created,” stated historian [Jessica Choppin
Roney](https://liberalarts.temple.edu/directory/jessica-choppin-
roney).[[6]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-6)

Years prior to the U.S. reach toward Alaska or Hawaii, and writing from Mount
Vernon on August 29, 1788, [George Washington
stated](https://archive.csac.history.wisc.edu/washington_to_newenham8.29.pdf),
“The natural, political, and moral circumstances of our nascent empire justify
the anticipation. We have an almost unbounded territory whose natural
advantages for agriculture & commerce [are] equal [to] those of any on the
globe.”[[7]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-7)
Further, [Thomas Jefferson in writing to James
Madison](https://www.loc.gov/exhibits/jefferson/149.html) from Monticello on
April 27, 1809, expressed “I [am] persuaded no constitution was ever before so
well calculated as ours for extensive empire & self-
government…”[[8]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-8)

In 1787, Alexander Hamilton wrote in _The Federalist Papers No. 1_ , “[To the
People of the State of New
York](https://avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/fed01.asp): The subject speaks
its own importance; comprehending in its consequences nothing less than the
existence of the Union, the safety and welfare of the parts of which it is
composed, the fate of an empire in many respects the most interesting in the
world…”[[9]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-9) In
other words, it was clear to Washington, Jefferson and Hamilton in these
exchanges that “empire” was an inevitable and desired component of an American
grand strategy. These outweighed notions of democracy and republicanism.

In yet another sequence, and writing from Paris on January 25, 1786, [Thomas
Jefferson wrote to Virginia attorney Archibald
Stuart](https://tjrs.monticello.org/letter/76) and stated:

> Our confederacy must be viewed as the nest from which all America, North and
> South is to be peopled. We should take care too not to think [about] it for
> the interest of that great continent to press too soon on the Spaniards.
> Those countries cannot be in better hands. My fear is that they are too
> feeble to hold them till our population can be sufficiently advanced to gain
> it from them [piece] by [piece]. The navigation of the Mississippi we must
> have.[[10]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-10)

Here, Jefferson’s writing explained the careful maintenance and intent that he
was prepared to undertake in structurally extending colonial violence in all
directions in coordination with the [Northwest
Ordinance](https://history.house.gov/Historical-Highlights/1700s/Northwest-
Ordinance-1787/).

[George Washington addressed New York lawyer James
Duane](https://teachingamericanhistory.org/document/letter-to-james-duane/) on
September 7, 1783, from Rocky Hill near Princeton, New Jersey, and said:

> At first view, it may seem a little extraneous, when I am called upon to
> give an opinion upon the terms of a Peace proper to be made with the
> Indians, that I should go into the formation of New States; but the
> [Settlement] -- of the Western Country and making a Peace with the Indians
> are so analogous that there can be no definition of the one without
> involving considerations of the other.

Washington continued:

> For I repeat it, again, and I am clear in my opinion, that policy and
> [economy] point very strongly to the expediency of being upon good terms
> with the Indians, and the propriety of purchasing their Lands in preference
> to attempting to drive them by force of arms out of their Country; which as
> we have already experienced is like driving the Wild Beasts of the Forest
> which will return to us soon as the pursuit is at an end and fall perhaps on
> those that are left there; -- when the gradual extension of our Settlements
> will as certainly cause the Savage as the Wolf to retire; both being beasts
> of prey [though] they differ in
> shape.[[11]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-11)

Washington’s poetics are horrific in its essential unambiguous language
driving at paternalism and ownership. Apologists for the First President and
[Father of the Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father_of_the_Nation)
might perceive the letter to be more about diplomacy, peacemaking and
peacekeeping when it is mostly written in a way that [Aimé
Césaire](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/aimae-fernand-caesaire) might
call decivilizing, dehumanizing, and with attempts in “thingifying” indigenous
people.[[12]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-12)

In writing from Washington D.C. on November 24, 1801, [Thomas Jefferson
addressed James Monroe](https://tjrs.monticello.org/letter/1743) stating:

> It is hard to believe that either Great Britain or the Indian proprietors
> have so disinterested or regard for us as to be willing to relieve us by
> receiving such a colony themselves; and as much to be doubted whether that
> race of men could long exist in so rigorous a climate. On our western and
> southern frontiers, Spain holds an immense country; the occupancy of which
> however is in the Indian nations; except a few insulated spots possessed by
> Spanish subjects -- It is very questionable indeed whether the Indians would
> sell? W[hether] Spain would be willing to receive these people?

Jefferson continued:

> And it was nearly certain that she would not alienate sovereignty. The same
> question to ourselves would recur here also, as did in the first case:
> should we be willing to have such a colony in contact with us? However our
> present interest may rest drain us within our own limits, it is possible not
> to look forward to distant times, when are rapid multiplication will expand
> itself beyond those limits, and cover the whole northern, if not southern
> continent with a people speaking the same language, governed in similar
> forms, and by similar laws: nor can we contemplate, with satisfaction,
> either blot or mixture on that surface.

Jefferson used even more stark and uncompromising language, in his letter to
John Adams on June 11, 1812, from
[Monticello](https://www.monticello.org/plan-your-visit-in-2026):

> The backward will yield and be thrown further back. These will relapse into
> barbarism & misery, lose numbers by war and want, and we shall be obliged to
> drive them, with the beasts of the forest, into the stony mountains. They
> will be conquered however in Canada. the possession of that country secures
> our women and children for ever from the tomahawk & scalping knife, by
> removing those who excite them.
> [[13]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-13)

Jefferson signifies his imperialist perspective and frames the removal and
subjugation of Indigenous peoples as necessary for territorial control and the
security of settlers. He makes it clear that he believes in racial
superiority, the separation of people, and the overall grand imperial project
that was based on a structurally and culturally violent law system. He wanted
a state that favored an English-speaking Anglo world and prioritized the use
of the American liberty project as an expansionary mechanism to set forth a
class based ethnic democracy.

Later on in 1823, Secretary of State John Quincy Adams observed that there are
“[laws of political gravitation](http://gtmoproject.umn.edu/slide1.php)” as
well as physical gravitation: “just as an apple, severed from its native tree,
must fall to the ground, so too would Cuba, forcibly separated from its
‘unnatural’ connection with Spain and incapable of self-support, gravitate
inevitably toward the North American
union.”[[14]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-14)
Later that year, President [James
Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Monroe), in his annual message to
Congress on December 2, articulated the principle of freedom for the American
continents from future European colonization. This policy became known as the
[Monroe
Doctrine](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1801-1829/monroe).[[15]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-15)

By 1824, supporters of [Andrew
Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson) celebrated him as
embodying the spirit of the American Revolution; he was running for the
presidency as a Democrat, and his campaign slogan was “[the glorious
principles of ’76](https://www.theamericanconservative.com/what-exactly-was-
the-spirit-
of-76/).[[16]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-16)
This was perhaps the beginning of early American populist attempts to
undermine elite imperial policies from the right.

Howard Zinn, author of the [_People’s History of the United
States_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_People%27s_History_of_the_United_States),
wrote about American exceptionalism and explained how in 1846, Democrats
ardently pushed expansion. The common phrase came from John O’Sullivan, editor
of the [_Democratic
Review_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_United_States_Magazine_and_Democratic_Review)
who in 1845 wrote, “our [manifest
destiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Progress#/media/File:American_Progress_\(John_Gast_painting\).jpg)
to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of
our yearly multiplying
millions.”[[17]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-17)
The idea of America guided by divine providence dates back to its separation
from Great Britain, when [John
Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams) articulated, “It was the will
of Heaven that the two countries should be
sundered.”[[18]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-18)

Leading up to the expansionary policies associated with the [Panama Canal’s
construction](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1899-1913/panama-canal) and
twentieth and twenty-first century warfare, there were additional annexation
projects. This long list of strategic territories included: Louisiana (1803),
Florida (1819), Republic of Texas (1845), Mexican Cession (1848), Gadsden
Purchase (1853), Alaska (1867), Hawaii (1898), Puerto Rico (1898), and just
after Panama, the Virgin Islands (1917). Prior to these all, however, were the
early American visions of continental empire, which helps to explain Trump’s
“[Donroe Doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donroe_Doctrine)” and
“[America First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America_First)” philosophy that
entails “[maximum pressure](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-
sheets/2025/02/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-restores-maximum-pressure-
on-iran/),” or what [Razi Canikligil](https://x.com/canikligil?lang=en) called
Trump’s pursuit of “a neo-imperialist
agenda.”[[19]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-19)
Further, on February 10, 2025, the _Financial Times_ called Trump, Xi, and
Putin committed expansionists in a “[new age of
empire](https://www.ft.com/content/8d1afb00-57ee-4b59-abe3-df0ff18084fb).”

Early American visions of continental empire gave us the imperial politics of
the current moment. Along with New World
“[discovery](https://www.cnn.com/2019/10/13/us/christopher-columbus-myth-
buster-trnd),” the colonial period, and prolonged chattel slavery, early
America led campaigns of Manifest Destiny and an intervention in Mexico. In
1832, the Democratic Party and a wing of the Jacksonians supported expansion
of U.S. territory through the annexation of
Texas.[[20]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-20)
Further calls for expansion could be seen in slogans such as “[Fifty-Four
Forty or Fight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_boundary_dispute),” the
1844 annexationist policy of James K. Polk who wanted the boundary line for
Oregon to be drawn at the latitude 54°
40’.[[21]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-21) Well
before Trump articulated a vision for projecting American renewed regional
hard power in the Panama Canal, Venezuela, Cuba, Greenland, and stretching to
[Gaza](https://www.cfr.org/articles/guide-trumps-twenty-point-gaza-peace-
deal), were elites of the aristocracy – enslavers and leaders such as George
Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Alexander Hamilton, and John Quincy Adams.
[[22]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-22) Their
private letters help to explain empire and the brutal mindset found in the
twenty-first century as we approach [America’s 250th
birthday](https://america250.org/).

Historian [Sophia Rosenfeld](https://www.thenation.com/article/world/the-
revolution-heard-around-the-world/) recently wrote:

> What a time to try to commemorate this nation’s founding! Imperialism is
> back. Militarized federal agents have been massing in cities to root out
> people deemed unwelcome or disloyal. The president styles himself more as a
> monarch than a civil servant, from the plans for his new golden ballroom to
> the parade of courtiers and oligarchs paying him homage. Given this
> situation, what are the options for narrating the story of the Declaration
> of Independence 250 years after the fact? Are we left with anything other
> than irony or tragedy?

The history of the United States from its founding through the early
nineteenth century exposes its [imperial
ambitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Ambitions).[[23]](https://www.counterpunch.org/feed/#post-416799-footnote-23)
This was not incidental, but central to the nation’s formation. Ranging from
Washington and Jefferson’s letters to the structuring of the [Northwest
Ordinance](https://news.osu.edu/scholars-gather-at-ohio-state-for-northwest-
ordinance-conference/), the dispossession and subjugation of indigenous
peoples were outlined as necessary for the growth of a continental republic.
Early American leaders consistently employed the rhetoric of liberty and the
strategies of territorial expansion. They set precedents for later policies of
[Manifest Destiny](https://www.wired.com/story/maga-manifest-destiny-
coalition/) and eventual intervention abroad. The Founders set racial
hierarchies and shaped the U.S. as inseparable from empire. Therefore,
America’s “[New Imperialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Imperialism)”
in the [global
south](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250753298/empiresworkshop/) was not
new at all. As America reaches its [250th](https://america250.org/) year, it
becomes clear that empire was not a departure from the aspirational democratic
ideals of 1776-1787; it was a parallel and continues in the
[present](https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-interactive/2026/jan/10/trump-
territorial-ambition-imperialism).
